turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. I've just been... well, it's been a long time coming, honestly. I manage a health clinic, and I've been doing this kind of work for years, so you'd think I'd have a handle on everything by now, right? But what finally pushed me to make this appointment and actually come in today is this... this absolute wall I keep hitting with my focus at work. 

It’s getting to the point where it's genuinely impacting my day-to-day. For example, I will sit down at my desk, close my office door so nobody bothers me, and open up an EPIC quality report. We have to do these constantly for compliance and clinic funding, so they are incredibly important. I sit there with every intention of tracking the data, going line by line, really digging into it. But I swear, within just a few minutes, my mind has drifted so far away. I'll suddenly snap back and realize I'm just staring at the monitor, rereading the exact same row of numbers over and over again without actually processing what any of it means. 

And it’s not just when I’m alone at my computer, either. It happens when I'm sitting right there in our clinic metrics meetings. We have these big discussions with the department heads, and I go in with my notepad, completely ready to track our performance and take charge, and then... I don't even know where my brain goes. I'll be looking right at the person presenting, and suddenly I realize I've completely missed the whole point of the discussion. It's so frustrating because I know how important these metrics are, and I want to pay attention, I really do, but it's like my brain just unplugs itself without my permission. And then I have to spend all this extra time trying to catch up or subtly piece together what we decided, which is just exhausting and, frankly, embarrassing at my level of management. So, I just felt like I couldn't keep ignoring it anymore.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly describes an inability to sustain attention during tasks like reading reports and attending meetings, noting that their mind drifts after just a few minutes.

turns.doctor_question: Do you remember having this same kind of trouble paying attention when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. Yes. In fact, it goes all the way back to when I was really little. I was actually just thinking about this recently because we were clearing out some old boxes at my parents' house, and... well, even in elementary school, I remember my teachers constantly writing the exact same things on my report cards. Every single year, it was always, "She is very bright, but she's careless." Or they'd say I wasn't working up to my potential because I'd miss these little details or make silly mistakes on things I actually knew how to do. 

And my mother... oh my goodness, my mother had the patience of an absolute saint. She literally had to sit right next to me at the kitchen table every single evening just to make sure I actually finished my homework. If she got up for even a second to stir a pot on the stove or answer the landline, I'd just drift off into my own world and completely stop working. Plus, it was always a whole exhausting production just to get started in the first place, because I would constantly lose track of what the actual assignments were. Or I would get all the way home off the bus and realize I had completely forgotten to bring my textbooks home from school. She'd ask where my math book was, and I'd just have this sinking feeling because I could picture it sitting right there inside my little wooden desk at school. 

It was so frustrating for her, and for me too, because I really wasn't trying to be difficult or rebellious. I just... things would just slip right out of my brain. She tried everything back then—buying me special color-coded folders, making little written checklists for me to check off before I left the classroom—but honestly, I'd usually end up losing the checklists too! So she just resorted to sitting there, physically anchoring me to the table until the work was done. It’s funny—well, not funny, really, but eye-opening—to look back now and realize that the way I felt sitting at that kitchen table when I was eight years old is the exact same way I feel now staring at my computer screen in my office. It’s like this lifelong thread of just... not being able to hold onto my own focus, no matter how hard I try.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient recalls teachers noting she would miss little details and make silly, careless mistakes.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes drifting off and stopping work if her mother wasn't sitting with her, and an ongoing inability to hold focus.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient needed her mother to sit with her every evening just to ensure she actually finished her homework.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions she would frequently end up losing the checklists her mother made for her.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient frequently forgot to bring her textbooks home from school and lost track of her assignments.
